currentProblem.name: The Halting Problem
currentProblem.description: Given encoding ⟨M, w⟩ of a Turing machine M and string w, determine whether M halts on input w.
currentProblem.inputFormat: ⟨M, w⟩ — finite encoding of TM M paired with input string w ∈ Σ*
currentProblem.question: Does M halt on input w?
yesInstances: ⟨M_accept_ε, ε⟩ — machine that immediately accepts halts on empty input
⟨M_identity, 0110⟩ — machine that copies its input and halts
noInstances: ⟨M_loop_forever, ε⟩ — machine that moves right indefinitely never halts
⟨M_loop_on_0, 0⟩ — machine that loops whenever it reads a 0

currentMachine.name: Diagonalizer — the self-refuting machine
currentMachine.description: Constructed to derive a contradiction from the assumption that a halting decider H exists. On input ⟨M⟩ (any TM encoding), D constructs the pair ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and invokes the assumed decider H on it. D then does the OPPOSITE of what H predicts: if H says M halts on ⟨M⟩, D loops forever; if H says M loops on ⟨M⟩, D halts and accepts. This inversion is the diagonal move.

computationTrace.machine: D on input ⟨D⟩ — both cases lead to contradiction

steps.tapeContents: ⟨D, ⟨D⟩⟩ — H now runs on this input

steps.state: CASE A — H outputs accept (claims D halts on ⟨D⟩)
steps.tapeContents: D transitions to q_H_said_halts_so_loop → D now LOOPS
H said D halts on ⟨D⟩, but D actually loops on ⟨D⟩. H is wrong.

steps.state: CASE B — H outputs reject (claims D loops on ⟨D⟩)
steps.tapeContents: D transitions to q_accept → D now HALTS
H said D loops on ⟨D⟩, but D actually halts on ⟨D⟩. H is wrong.

computationTrace.terminationReason: Both possible outcomes produce a logical contradiction. No behavior D could exhibit is consistent with H's prediction. Therefore H cannot exist.

enumeration.description: Enumerate all Turing machines in lexicographic order by their encoding: M₁, M₂, M₃, … This is possible because every TM has a finite description over a finite alphabet, so TMs are countably infinite. Imagine an infinite boolean matrix T where T[i][j] = 1 if Mᵢ halts on input ⟨Mⱼ⟩, and 0 if Mᵢ loops on ⟨Mⱼ⟩. The DIAGONAL of this matrix — entries T[i][i] — records whether each machine halts on its OWN encoding. Machine D is constructed to INVERT every diagonal entry: D on ⟨Mᵢ⟩ does the opposite of what T[i][i] says. When D itself is in the enumeration at index k, entry T[k][k] must simultaneously equal both 0 and 1 — a contradiction. The matrix cannot exist, and neither can H.
enumeration.indexSet: ℕ (countably infinite — TM encodings are finite strings over {0,1}*)
enumeration.enumeratedObjects: All Turing machines M₁, M₂, M₃, … indexed by their canonical encoding

reductionFunction.description: Supplement the ATM undecidability result: if HALT_TM were decidable, we could decide ATM by first checking if M halts on w, then simulating M. This shows HALT_TM is at least as hard as ATM.
reductionFunction.inputTransformation: From ⟨M, w⟩ for ATM, construct ⟨M', w⟩ where M' simulates M but converts reject into a loop (so M' halts iff M accepts).
reductionFunction.outputInterpretation: HALT_TM(M', w) = accept iff ATM(M, w) = accept.
reductionFunction.preserves: yes/no answers — membership in ATM iff membership in modified HALT_TM instance

dependencies: Turing (1936) — 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem'
Church-Turing thesis — TMs capture all effective computation
Universal Turing Machine (UTM) — a TM that simulates any other TM on any input
TM encodings are countable — every TM has a finite description; Σ* is countable
Definition of a decider — a TM that halts on ALL inputs (not just yes-instances)
Cantor's diagonalization technique (1891) — the logical ancestor of Turing's argument
assumptions: Church-Turing thesis: every effectively computable function is computable by some Turing machine
Every Turing machine has a finite, canonical encoding over a finite alphabet
A decider must halt on EVERY input and always output accept or reject — looping is not allowed
Self-reference is syntactically valid: feeding ⟨M⟩ as input to M is a legal TM computation
The assumed decider H, if it existed, would be a total (always-halting) TM
keyInsight: The proof is a proof by contradiction structured as a diagonalization. Assume total decider H for HALT_TM exists. Construct D: on ⟨M⟩, run H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and do the opposite (loop if H says halt; halt if H says loop). Now ask: what does D do on ⟨D⟩? D halts on ⟨D⟩ ⟺ H rejects ⟨D, ⟨D⟩⟩ ⟺ D loops on ⟨D⟩. Contradiction in both directions. The diagonal move — disagreeing with every machine on its own encoding — guarantees D cannot appear in any decision table, proving H cannot exist. Note: HALT_TM is still SEMI-decidable (a UTM accepts ⟨M,w⟩ when M halts, but loops forever when M loops), so 'undecidable' ≠ 'no insight is ever possible.'
